extracted.intended_audience: Authors and referees (especially PhD students, junior faculty, and development economists) preparing submissions to or reviewing for top economics journals such as the QJE.
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice from the QJE editor on how manuscripts are screened, what makes a paper suitable for refereeing, expectations for referee reports, revision standards, data/registration norms, and tips for interdisciplinary submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial screening / send-to-referees standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Only send a paper out to referees if it has great promise to be a significant contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors perform a tough initial screen because the journal receives many submissions but publishes few papers (QJE desk rejected ~62% of new submissions in 2011). A paper should show clear potential for significance before being sent to referees; otherwise it will likely be desk rejected. Editors typically read the paper within a day and decide whether to send it out or desk reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk-reject triggers: sloppiness and unreadability
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper will get desk rejected for sure if it is sloppy (missing references, tables and figures that can’t be deciphered, equations with notation that is not defined, poor and verbose writing, etc.) regardless of the quality of the ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation matters: ensure complete references, legible tables/figures, defined notation, and clear, concise prose. Even strong ideas can be desk rejected if the manuscript is not polished and readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript readiness / timing of submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Young scholars should NOT submit a paper to a top journal too soon. You should only submit polished work that has been presented several times and incorporated the critical feedback of colleagues and/or advisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present drafts, get critical feedback, and revise thoroughly before submitting to a top journal. Submitting too early closes off options and reduces chance of getting past initial screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee report structure: start with a concise summary and be critical but polite
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should provide a concise summary of the paper they review at the start of their report and then provide a critical but polite evaluation of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin reports with a short summary so the editor and author understand the referee's reading of the contribution. Maintain a professional, constructive tone even when critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: No editorial recommendation in the referee report (use separate cover letter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The referee report itself should not include an explicit editorial recommendation. That recommendation should be in a separate cover letter to the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the body of the referee report focused on assessment and detailed comments; convey accept/reject/revise recommendations to the editor via the designated cover-letter channel to preserve report utility and editorial confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of comments should match likelihood of recommending revision
rubrics_metrics.description: The more likely you think the paper is to merit a revision the more detailed should be the comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you believe a paper merits revision, provide a roadmap of what to change and detailed suggestions. For papers that are clear rejects, shorter reports are acceptable and often preferable if timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness expectation for referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports should be done in a timely manner (4 weeks is our expected due date); the editor's median turnaround for referee reports is 33 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot meet the deadline, decline promptly rather than accept and deliver late. A brief but timely rejection report is better than a delayed, detailed one. Editors monitor reports closely and act quickly when reports arrive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors may act on initial referee reports without waiting for all reports
rubrics_metrics.description: QJE editors monitor the refereeing process and look at each referee report as it comes in rather than waiting for all the reports to have been completed. Thus, if the initial referee reports received recommend rejection and are convincing, the editor makes a rejection decision without waiting for all the reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should be aware that early, convincing reports can determine the outcome; providing clear, well-argued assessments promptly influences editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise-and-resubmit letters should be precise and provide a roadmap
rubrics_metrics.description: Our revise and resubmit letters try to be as precise as possible in providing authors with a road map to what changes need to be made (and which of the referees’ suggestions should be followed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors aim to tell authors exactly which changes are required and which referee suggestions are important. Authors should respond directly and comprehensively to those points; a responsive, serious revision is likely to be accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: High threshold for requesting major revisions / conditional acceptance practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The hurdle for asking for a revision is quite high at the QJE since we can only publish a small share of the papers sent out to referees. Once a revision has been received, we typically send it back to the most relevant subset of referees and then make an up-or-down decision on the first revision. Any further rounds after this “conditional acceptance” involve minor (but essential) revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that revise-and-resubmit requests are for papers with substantial promise; authors should treat such invitations seriously and produce focused, comprehensive revisions because acceptance decisions are often made on the first revised submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report concision and suitability for junior referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Young referees should avoid overenthusiastic, overly long reports. The referee report itself should be concise, with more detail provided only when recommending revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junior referees should prioritize clarity and brevity. If a paper is likely to be a reject, a short, prompt report is more useful than a long delayed critique. Save long, exhaustive commentary for papers you believe merit revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a paper of general interest: innovation and broader lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: The country (or countries) being studied is not that relevant for whether a paper is considered of general interest. The degree of methodological and substantive innovation and the quality of the ideas and research are what matter. It is reasonable to try to provide readers with some sense in the introduction and conclusion of the broader (but direct) lessons that can be distilled from one’s research. But one should not go off the deep end in doing this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on methodological/substantive innovation and clearly articulate the broader, directly supported lessons in intro/conclusion without overstating generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: External validity and replication expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of external validity need to be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Replication studies are important, but it is unlikely many pure replication studies will be published in major economics journals unless they generate new lessons (e.g., which policies replicate and which ones don’t or something systematic about what settings do or don’t generate larger treatment effects). Single replication studies just are not that exciting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replication work should aim to provide new insights or systematic comparisons (not merely repeat a result). Authors should make explicit arguments about external validity and, where relevant, discuss what additional lessons their replication yields. Be mindful of multiple hypothesis testing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registry and data availability norms for randomized experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathetic to creating a registry for randomized field experiments and for laboratory experiments in economics to improve transparency and provide opportunities for sticking to a pre-analysis plan. I would hope the QJE would follow the guidelines set by AEA journals in encouraging such registration of submitted papers. Making one’s data available to other researchers to the extent possible given human subjects concerns is also important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors of randomized trials should register experiments and pre-analysis plans where appropriate, and share data subject to human-subjects/privacy constraints. Editors recognize practical issues (distinguishing trials from natural experiments; government-run programs) and allow case-by-case consideration for ex post analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary submissions to medical journals: need experienced collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Any economist trying to submit to a major medical journal needs a collaborator with experience in publishing in medical journals and in responding to the referees at medical journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming for biomedical journals, partner with coauthors familiar with those journals’ conventions, templates, and review expectations to navigate the different length/format/review norms effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' communication style: be direct, polite, and constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: I try to be direct but as polite and constructive as possible in rejection letters. I also try to provide authors with some brief feedback on their papers and the rationale for the decision even in the case of desk rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can expect clear reasons when rejected; editors aim to give constructive guidance. When writing to authors (e.g., rebuttals or resubmissions), maintain a polite, professional tone that addresses editors' and referees' points directly.
